Let \(\vec{P} = 2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+3\hat{k}\) and \(\vec{Q} = -5\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-5\hat{k}\) be the position vectors of P and Q.
R divides PQ internally in the ratio 3 : 2, so by the section formula,
\(\vec{R} = \dfrac{3\vec{Q}+2\vec{P}}{3+2}\)
\(= \dfrac{3(-5\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-5\hat{k})+2(2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+3\hat{k})}{5}\)
\(= \dfrac{(-15+4)\hat{i}+(6-2)\hat{j}+(-15+6)\hat{k}}{5}\)
\(= \dfrac{-11\hat{i}+4\hat{j}-9\hat{k}}{5}\)
**Position vector of R (internal division) \(= -\dfrac{11}{5}\hat{i}+\dfrac{4}{5}\hat{j}-\dfrac{9}{5}\hat{k}\)**

Let \(\vec{P} = 2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+3\hat{k}\) and \(\vec{Q} = -5\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-5\hat{k}\) be the position vectors of P and Q.
R divides PQ externally in the ratio 3 : 2, so by the section formula for external division,
\(\vec{R} = \dfrac{3\vec{Q}-2\vec{P}}{3-2}\)
\(= 3(-5\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-5\hat{k}) - 2(2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+3\hat{k})\)
\(= (-15-4)\hat{i}+(6+2)\hat{j}+(-15-6)\hat{k}\)
**Position vector of R (external division) \(= -19\hat{i}+8\hat{j}-21\hat{k}\)**

Let O be the origin and let \(\vec{a}=\overrightarrow{OA}\), \(\vec{b}=\overrightarrow{OB}\).
Since E is the mid-point of OB, \(\vec{E}=\dfrac{\vec{b}}{2}\).
Since AD : DB = 2 : 1, D divides AB so that \(\vec{D}=\dfrac{2\vec{b}+1\cdot\vec{a}}{2+1}=\dfrac{\vec{a}+2\vec{b}}{3}\).
Let P divide OD in the ratio \(t:(1-t)\) from O, i.e. \(\vec{P}=t\vec{D}=\dfrac{t}{3}(\vec{a}+2\vec{b})\), and let P divide AE in the ratio \(s:(1-s)\) from A: \(\vec{P}=(1-s)\vec{a}+\dfrac{s}{2}\vec{b}\).
Since \(\vec{a},\vec{b}\) are independent, equate coefficients:
\(\dfrac{t}{3}=1-s\) and \(\dfrac{2t}{3}=\dfrac{s}{2}\Rightarrow s=\dfrac{4t}{3}\)
Substituting: \(\dfrac{t}{3}=1-\dfrac{4t}{3}\Rightarrow \dfrac{5t}{3}=1\Rightarrow t=\dfrac{3}{5}\)
Since \(\vec{P}=t\vec{D}\) with \(t=\dfrac{3}{5}\), P divides OD such that \(OP=\dfrac{3}{5}OD\) and \(PD=\dfrac{2}{5}OD\).
**\(OP:PD = 3:2\)**

Let O(0,0,0) be a vertex of the tetrahedron OABC with A(a, 2, 3), B(1, b, 2), C(2, 1, c).
The centroid of a tetrahedron is the average of the position vectors of its four vertices:
\(G=\left(\dfrac{0+a+1+2}{4},\dfrac{0+2+b+1}{4},\dfrac{0+3+2+c}{4}\right)=\left(\dfrac{a+3}{4},\dfrac{b+3}{4},\dfrac{c+5}{4}\right)\)
Given \(G=(1,2,-1)\), so
\(\dfrac{a+3}{4}=1\Rightarrow a=1\)
\(\dfrac{b+3}{4}=2\Rightarrow b=5\)
\(\dfrac{c+5}{4}=-1\Rightarrow c=-9\)
So \(P(a,b,c)=P(1,5,-9)\).
Distance of P from the origin \(=\sqrt{1^2+5^2+(-9)^2}=\sqrt{1+25+81}=\sqrt{107}\)
**Required distance \(=\sqrt{107}\) units**

The centroid of a tetrahedron with vertices K, L, M, N is the average of their position vectors:
\(G=\dfrac{\vec{K}+\vec{L}+\vec{M}+\vec{N}}{4}\)
\(=\left(\dfrac{5+1+4+6}{4},\dfrac{-7+5-6-4}{4},\dfrac{0+3+3+2}{4}\right)\)
\(=\left(\dfrac{16}{4},\dfrac{-12}{4},\dfrac{8}{4}\right)\)
**Centroid \(=(4,-3,2)\)**

Position vectors of L and N are \(\vec{L}=7\hat{i}-6\hat{j}+12\hat{k}\) and \(\vec{N}=5\hat{i}+4\hat{j}-2\hat{k}\).
Since M is the mid-point of LN,
\(\vec{M}=\dfrac{\vec{L}+\vec{N}}{2}=\dfrac{(7+5)\hat{i}+(-6+4)\hat{j}+(12-2)\hat{k}}{2}\)
\(=\dfrac{12\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+10\hat{k}}{2}\)
**\(\vec{M}=6\hat{i}-\hat{j}+5\hat{k}\), i.e. \(M(6,-1,5)\)**

Since A, B, C are collinear, C lies on line AB, so \(\overrightarrow{C}=\overrightarrow{A}+t(\overrightarrow{B}-\overrightarrow{A})\) for some scalar t.
Using the x-coordinates (the only coordinate free of the unknowns p, q):
\(-3 = 3+t(-1-3)=3-4t\)
\(\Rightarrow 4t=6\Rightarrow t=\dfrac{3}{2}\)
Since \(t=\dfrac{3}{2}>1\), C lies beyond B on line AB, so C divides AB externally.
\(AC = t\cdot AB=\dfrac{3}{2}AB\) and \(CB=(t-1)AB=\dfrac{1}{2}AB\), so
\(AC:CB=\dfrac{3}{2}:\dfrac{1}{2}=3:1\)
**C divides AB externally in the ratio 3 : 1**

From part (i), C divides AB externally in the ratio 3 : 1, so by the section formula for external division,
\(\overrightarrow{C}=\dfrac{3\overrightarrow{B}-1\cdot\overrightarrow{A}}{3-1}=\dfrac{3\overrightarrow{B}-\overrightarrow{A}}{2}\)
Using the y-coordinate: \(3=\dfrac{3q-0}{2}\Rightarrow 3q=6\Rightarrow q=2\)
Using the z-coordinate: \(0=\dfrac{3(3)-p}{2}\Rightarrow 9-p=0\Rightarrow p=9\)
**\(p=9,\ q=2\)**

C divides AB in the ratio 3 : 2, so by the section formula,
\(\overrightarrow{C}=\dfrac{3\overrightarrow{B}+2\overrightarrow{A}}{3+2}\)
\(=\dfrac{3(\vec{a}-3\vec{b})+2(6\vec{a}+2\vec{b})}{5}\)
\(=\dfrac{3\vec{a}-9\vec{b}+12\vec{a}+4\vec{b}}{5}\)
\(=\dfrac{15\vec{a}-5\vec{b}}{5}\)
\(=3\vec{a}-\vec{b}\)
**Hence the position vector of C is \(3\vec{a}-\vec{b}\), as required.**

Let ABCD be a quadrilateral with position vectors \(\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c},\vec{d}\).
Let P, Q, R, S be the mid-points of AB, BC, CD, DA respectively:
\(\vec{P}=\dfrac{\vec{a}+\vec{b}}{2},\ \vec{Q}=\dfrac{\vec{b}+\vec{c}}{2},\ \vec{R}=\dfrac{\vec{c}+\vec{d}}{2},\ \vec{S}=\dfrac{\vec{d}+\vec{a}}{2}\)
Then
\(\overrightarrow{PQ}=\vec{Q}-\vec{P}=\dfrac{\vec{c}-\vec{a}}{2}\)
\(\overrightarrow{SR}=\vec{R}-\vec{S}=\dfrac{\vec{c}-\vec{a}}{2}\)
Since \(\overrightarrow{PQ}=\overrightarrow{SR}\), PQ is parallel to SR and \(|PQ|=|SR|\).
**Hence PQRS is a parallelogram, i.e. the line segments joining the mid-points of adjacent sides of a quadrilateral form a parallelogram.**

Let \(\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}\) be the position vectors of A, B, C. D divides BC in the ratio 2 : 3, so
\(\vec{D}=\dfrac{2\vec{c}+3\vec{b}}{5}\)
E divides CA in the ratio 2 : 3, so
\(\vec{E}=\dfrac{2\vec{a}+3\vec{c}}{5}\)
Let the point of intersection P divide AD in the ratio \(t:(1-t)\) from A: \(\vec{P}=(1-t)\vec{a}+t\vec{D}\), and let it divide BE in the ratio \(s:(1-s)\) from B: \(\vec{P}=(1-s)\vec{b}+s\vec{E}\).
Expanding,
\(\vec{P}=(1-t)\vec{a}+\dfrac{3t}{5}\vec{b}+\dfrac{2t}{5}\vec{c}\)
\(\vec{P}=\dfrac{2s}{5}\vec{a}+(1-s)\vec{b}+\dfrac{3s}{5}\vec{c}\)
Equating coefficients of \(\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}\):
\(1-t=\dfrac{2s}{5}\), \(\dfrac{3t}{5}=1-s\), \(\dfrac{2t}{5}=\dfrac{3s}{5}\Rightarrow s=\dfrac{2t}{3}\)
Substituting into the second equation: \(\dfrac{3t}{5}=1-\dfrac{2t}{3}\Rightarrow \dfrac{9t+10t}{15}=1\Rightarrow t=\dfrac{15}{19}\), and \(s=\dfrac{10}{19}\)
So \(AP:PD=t:(1-t)=15:4\) and \(BP:PE=s:(1-s)=10:9\).
Position vector of P:
\(\vec{P}=(1-t)\vec{a}+\dfrac{3t}{5}\vec{b}+\dfrac{2t}{5}\vec{c}=\dfrac{4}{19}\vec{a}+\dfrac{9}{19}\vec{b}+\dfrac{6}{19}\vec{c}\)
**\(\vec{P}=\dfrac{4\vec{a}+9\vec{b}+6\vec{c}}{19}\); P divides AD in the ratio 15 : 4 and BE in the ratio 10 : 9.**

Let ABCD be a quadrilateral with position vectors \(\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c},\vec{d}\).
**(⇒) If ABCD is a parallelogram, then diagonals bisect each other:**
Since ABCD is a parallelogram, \(\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{DC}\), i.e. \(\vec{b}-\vec{a}=\vec{c}-\vec{d}\), so \(\vec{a}+\vec{c}=\vec{b}+\vec{d}\).
Mid-point of AC \(=\dfrac{\vec{a}+\vec{c}}{2}\) and mid-point of BD \(=\dfrac{\vec{b}+\vec{d}}{2}\). Since \(\vec{a}+\vec{c}=\vec{b}+\vec{d}\), these mid-points coincide, so diagonals AC and BD bisect each other.
**(⇐) If the diagonals bisect each other, then ABCD is a parallelogram:**
Let diagonals AC and BD bisect each other at M. Then
\(\dfrac{\vec{a}+\vec{c}}{2}=\dfrac{\vec{b}+\vec{d}}{2}\Rightarrow \vec{a}+\vec{c}=\vec{b}+\vec{d}\Rightarrow \vec{b}-\vec{a}=\vec{c}-\vec{d}\)
That is, \(\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{DC}\), so AB is parallel to DC and \(|AB|=|DC|\). Hence ABCD is a parallelogram.
**Hence a quadrilateral is a parallelogram if and only if its diagonals bisect each other.**

Let ABCD be a trapezium with \(AB \parallel DC\), so \(\overrightarrow{AB}=k\cdot\overrightarrow{DC}\) for some scalar \(k>0\), i.e. \(\vec{b}-\vec{a}=k(\vec{c}-\vec{d})\).
Let E and F be the mid-points of the non-parallel sides AD and BC, so that EF is the median of the trapezium:
\(\vec{E}=\dfrac{\vec{a}+\vec{d}}{2},\qquad \vec{F}=\dfrac{\vec{b}+\vec{c}}{2}\)
Then
\(\overrightarrow{EF}=\vec{F}-\vec{E}=\dfrac{(\vec{b}-\vec{a})+(\vec{c}-\vec{d})}{2}=\dfrac{k(\vec{c}-\vec{d})+(\vec{c}-\vec{d})}{2}=\dfrac{k+1}{2}(\vec{c}-\vec{d})\)
Since \(\overrightarrow{EF}\) is a scalar multiple of \(\overrightarrow{DC}=\vec{c}-\vec{d}\), EF is parallel to DC (and hence to AB).
Taking magnitudes: \(|EF|=\dfrac{k+1}{2}|DC|=\dfrac{k|DC|+|DC|}{2}=\dfrac{|AB|+|DC|}{2}\) (since \(|AB|=k|DC|\))
**Hence the median of a trapezium is parallel to its parallel sides, and its length equals half the sum of the lengths of the parallel sides.**

Let the third vertex be C(x, y, z). Since the centroid of \(\triangle ABC\) is the average of the vertices,
\(G=\left(\dfrac{3+(-4)+x}{3},\dfrac{1+5+y}{3},\dfrac{4+(-3)+z}{3}\right)=(-1,2,1)\)
Equating coordinates:
\(\dfrac{-1+x}{3}=-1\Rightarrow x=-2\)
\(\dfrac{6+y}{3}=2\Rightarrow y=0\)
\(\dfrac{1+z}{3}=1\Rightarrow z=2\)
**C = (–2, 0, 2)**

Let \(\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}\) be the position vectors of A, B, C. Since D, E, F are the mid-points of BC, CA, AB,
\(\vec{D}=\dfrac{\vec{b}+\vec{c}}{2},\quad \vec{E}=\dfrac{\vec{c}+\vec{a}}{2},\quad \vec{F}=\dfrac{\vec{a}+\vec{b}}{2}\)
Then
\(\overrightarrow{AD}=\vec{D}-\vec{a}=\dfrac{\vec{b}+\vec{c}-2\vec{a}}{2}\)
\(\overrightarrow{BE}=\vec{E}-\vec{b}=\dfrac{\vec{c}+\vec{a}-2\vec{b}}{2}\)
\(\overrightarrow{CF}=\vec{F}-\vec{c}=\dfrac{\vec{a}+\vec{b}-2\vec{c}}{2}\)
Adding,
\(\overrightarrow{AD}+\overrightarrow{BE}+\overrightarrow{CF}=\dfrac{(\vec{b}+\vec{c}-2\vec{a})+(\vec{c}+\vec{a}-2\vec{b})+(\vec{a}+\vec{b}-2\vec{c})}{2}=\dfrac{\vec{0}}{2}=\vec{0}\)
**Hence \(\overrightarrow{AD}+\overrightarrow{BE}+\overrightarrow{CF}=\vec{0}\), as required.**

Let \(\vec{A}=-\hat{i}+6\hat{j}+5\hat{k}\) and let \(\vec{B}\) be the position vector of B. Since P divides AB internally in the ratio 3 : 2,
\(\vec{P}=\dfrac{3\vec{B}+2\vec{A}}{5}\Rightarrow \vec{B}=\dfrac{5\vec{P}-2\vec{A}}{3}\)
Here \(5\vec{P}=-14\hat{i}+39\hat{j}+28\hat{k}\) and \(2\vec{A}=-2\hat{i}+12\hat{j}+10\hat{k}\), so
\(5\vec{P}-2\vec{A}=(-14+2)\hat{i}+(39-12)\hat{j}+(28-10)\hat{k}=-12\hat{i}+27\hat{j}+18\hat{k}\)
\(\vec{B}=\dfrac{-12\hat{i}+27\hat{j}+18\hat{k}}{3}=-4\hat{i}+9\hat{j}+6\hat{k}\)
**B = (–4, 9, 6)**

Let ABC be a triangle with position vectors \(\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}\), and let D, E, F be the mid-points of BC, CA, AB respectively, so that AD, BE, CF are the three medians.
\(\vec{D}=\dfrac{\vec{b}+\vec{c}}{2},\quad \vec{E}=\dfrac{\vec{c}+\vec{a}}{2},\quad \vec{F}=\dfrac{\vec{a}+\vec{b}}{2}\)
The median vectors directed from the vertices are
\(\overrightarrow{AD}=\dfrac{\vec{b}+\vec{c}-2\vec{a}}{2},\quad \overrightarrow{BE}=\dfrac{\vec{c}+\vec{a}-2\vec{b}}{2},\quad \overrightarrow{CF}=\dfrac{\vec{a}+\vec{b}-2\vec{c}}{2}\)
Adding these,
\(\overrightarrow{AD}+\overrightarrow{BE}+\overrightarrow{CF}=\dfrac{(\vec{b}+\vec{c}-2\vec{a})+(\vec{c}+\vec{a}-2\vec{b})+(\vec{a}+\vec{b}-2\vec{c})}{2}=\dfrac{\vec{0}}{2}=\vec{0}\)
**Hence the sum of the three vectors determined by the medians of a triangle, directed from the vertices, is zero.**

Take A as the origin, and let \(\vec{b}=\overrightarrow{AB},\ \vec{d}=\overrightarrow{AD}\). Since ABCD is a parallelogram, \(\overrightarrow{AC}=\vec{b}+\vec{d}\), so C has position vector \(\vec{b}+\vec{d}\).
E is the mid-point of BC: \(\vec{E}=\dfrac{\vec{b}+(\vec{b}+\vec{d})}{2}=\vec{b}+\dfrac{\vec{d}}{2}\)
F is the mid-point of CD: \(\vec{F}=\dfrac{(\vec{b}+\vec{d})+\vec{d}}{2}=\dfrac{\vec{b}}{2}+\vec{d}\)
**Finding Q (intersection of AE with diagonal BD):**
Points on AE: \(t\vec{E}=t\vec{b}+\dfrac{t}{2}\vec{d}\). Points on BD, from B to D: \(\vec{b}+u(\vec{d}-\vec{b})=(1-u)\vec{b}+u\vec{d}\)
Equating coefficients: \(t=1-u\) and \(\dfrac{t}{2}=u\). Solving, \(u=\dfrac{1}{3}\), \(t=\dfrac{2}{3}\).
So \(BQ:QD=u:(1-u)=1:2\), i.e. \(BQ=\dfrac{1}{3}BD\).
**Finding P (intersection of AF with diagonal BD):**
Points on AF: \(s\vec{F}=\dfrac{s}{2}\vec{b}+s\vec{d}\). Equating with \((1-u')\vec{b}+u'\vec{d}\): \(\dfrac{s}{2}=1-u'\) and \(s=u'\).
Solving, \(s=\dfrac{2}{3}\), \(u'=\dfrac{2}{3}\), so \(BP:PD=u':(1-u')=2:1\), i.e. \(BP=\dfrac{2}{3}BD\).
Thus, going from B to D: \(BQ=\dfrac{1}{3}BD\), \(QP=BP-BQ=\dfrac{2}{3}BD-\dfrac{1}{3}BD=\dfrac{1}{3}BD\), \(PD=BD-BP=\dfrac{1}{3}BD\)
**Since \(BQ=QP=PD=\dfrac{1}{3}BD\), the points P and Q trisect DB.**

Take the circumcenter Q as the origin, so \(\vec{a}=\overrightarrow{QA},\ \vec{b}=\overrightarrow{QB},\ \vec{c}=\overrightarrow{QC}\) all have equal magnitude \(|\vec{a}|=|\vec{b}|=|\vec{c}|=R\) (the circumradius).
Claim: the point H with position vector \(\vec{h}=\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}\) (relative to Q) is the orthocenter.
Check \(AH \perp BC\): \(\overrightarrow{AH}=\vec{h}-\vec{a}=\vec{b}+\vec{c}\) and \(\overrightarrow{BC}=\vec{c}-\vec{b}\)
\(\overrightarrow{AH}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}=(\vec{b}+\vec{c})\cdot(\vec{c}-\vec{b})=|\vec{c}|^2-|\vec{b}|^2=R^2-R^2=0\)
So \(AH\perp BC\); similarly \(BH\perp CA\) and \(CH\perp AB\). Hence H (position vector \(\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}\)) is the orthocenter, so \(P\equiv H\) and \(\overrightarrow{QP}=\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}\).
Now,
\(\overrightarrow{PA}=\vec{a}-\overrightarrow{QP}=-(\vec{b}+\vec{c})\)
\(\overrightarrow{PB}=\vec{b}-\overrightarrow{QP}=-(\vec{a}+\vec{c})\)
\(\overrightarrow{PC}=\vec{c}-\overrightarrow{QP}=-(\vec{a}+\vec{b})\)
Adding,
\(\overrightarrow{PA}+\overrightarrow{PB}+\overrightarrow{PC}=-2(\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c})=-2\overrightarrow{QP}=2\overrightarrow{PQ}\)
(since \(\overrightarrow{PQ}=-\overrightarrow{QP}\))
**Hence \(\overrightarrow{PA}+\overrightarrow{PC}+\overrightarrow{PB}=2\overrightarrow{PQ}\), as required.**

As in the previous result, take the circumcenter Q as the origin, with \(\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}\) the position vectors of A, B, C (\(|\vec{a}|=|\vec{b}|=|\vec{c}|=R\)). The orthocenter P then has position vector
\(\overrightarrow{QP}=\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}\)
(verified by checking \(AH\perp BC\), \(BH\perp CA\), \(CH\perp AB\) for the point H with this position vector).
The centroid G of \(\triangle ABC\) has position vector
\(\overrightarrow{QG}=\dfrac{\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}}{3}\)
Therefore,
\(3\overrightarrow{QG}=\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}=\overrightarrow{QP}\)
**Hence \(\overrightarrow{QP}=3\overrightarrow{QG}\), as required.** (This also shows Q, G, P are collinear — the Euler line of the triangle.)

Let \(\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}\) be the position vectors of A, B, C. Since P is the mid-point of AB,
\(\vec{P}=\dfrac{\vec{a}+\vec{b}}{2}\)
So,
\(\overrightarrow{PC}=\vec{c}-\vec{P}=\vec{c}-\dfrac{\vec{a}+\vec{b}}{2}=\dfrac{2\vec{c}-\vec{a}-\vec{b}}{2}\)
**\(\overrightarrow{PC}=\dfrac{2\vec{c}-\vec{a}-\vec{b}}{2}\)**

Let O be the origin and let \(\vec{a}=\overrightarrow{OA}\), \(\vec{b}=\overrightarrow{OB}\).
Since E is the mid-point of BO (the same point as the mid-point of OB), \(\vec{E}=\dfrac{\vec{b}}{2}\).
Since AD : DB = 2 : 1, D divides AB so that \(\vec{D}=\dfrac{2\vec{b}+\vec{a}}{3}\).
Let P divide OD in the ratio \(t:(1-t)\) from O: \(\vec{P}=t\vec{D}=\dfrac{t}{3}(\vec{a}+2\vec{b})\), and let P divide AE in the ratio \(s:(1-s)\) from A: \(\vec{P}=(1-s)\vec{a}+\dfrac{s}{2}\vec{b}\)
Since \(\vec{a},\vec{b}\) are independent, equate coefficients:
\(\dfrac{t}{3}=1-s\) and \(\dfrac{2t}{3}=\dfrac{s}{2}\Rightarrow s=\dfrac{4t}{3}\)
Substituting: \(\dfrac{t}{3}=1-\dfrac{4t}{3}\Rightarrow \dfrac{5t}{3}=1\Rightarrow t=\dfrac{3}{5}\)
Since \(\vec{P}=\dfrac{3}{5}\vec{D}\), P divides OD such that \(OP=\dfrac{3}{5}OD\) and \(PD=\dfrac{2}{5}OD\)
**\(OP:PD=3:2\)**
